data.title: ‘GTA VI’ to supercharge Sony — but not so much in Japan
data.description:
Arriving after a 13-year wait, the release of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ has created a global gaming buzz, but it might fail to leave its mark on the gaming capital of the world

The global launch of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) on Thursday provided a major boost to PlayStation maker Sony, although in its home market of Japan, the franchise remains a niche pursuit.

The long-awaited open-world crime action game from Take-Two Interactive’s Rockstar Games is rolling out across the world and has been met with rave reviews and fans taking time off work to play.

About three-quarters of the 17 million GTA VI units sold are on PlayStation, according to estimates from Sensor Tower, outselling Xbox maker Microsoft.

Shares in Sony, whose PlayStation 5 console is in its seventh year on the market, were up almost 3 percent in Tokyo compared with flat trading in the benchmark index. The shares had sold off on concern its business might be disrupted by artificial intelligence (AI) and supply chain snarls, but have rebounded in the past few months.

Analysts think the global enthusiasm is unlikely to reach a fever pitch in Japan, where Switch 2 maker Nintendo dominates the gaming device market and consumers prefer anime-style titles to realistic, violent Western games.

“The current trends in Japan don’t really fit this kind of game,” Toyo Securities analyst Hideki Yasuda said.

Given worldwide demand, “there’s absolutely no need for this game to sell in Japan,” he said.

Earlier this year, Sony scored a major global success with the movie Spider-Man: Brand New Day, but in Japan faced competition from breakout hit Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of Mermaid Island.

“A few of my friends bought GTA VI at midnight, but I’m in no hurry to as it’s only on PS5 and Xbox and you can’t play multiplayer online yet,” said Sorataka Goto, 33, who was shopping in Tokyo’s Akihabara electronics district.

“If and when it’s on PC and you can play online I’ll consider buying it,” said Goto, who bought the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

Nintendo has sold more than 5 million copies of the Switch 2 title, which was originally on the Nintendo 64, in the first four days since its launch earlier this month.

“I had the original as a child and so was excited to try this version,” he said.

Gamers in Japan might struggle to fully understand the satirical elements of GTA VI, the references to the Florida lifestyle and Western memes, said Serkan Toto, founder of game industry consultancy Kantan Games.

Still, the worldwide hype for GTA VI is spilling over to Japan and marketing in the country is unprecedented for a Western-made game, he said.

In Akihabara, a large poster featuring the lead characters, Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, was plastered on the side of a building.

“GTA VI will not become a mega blockbuster in Japan but it will do very, very well,” Toto said.

Analysts expect the release of GTA VI to soften the decline of PS5 hardware sales this year and support growth in software sales. Console sales are cyclical, with some observers expecting a successor gaming device in late 2028.

Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 units during the July to September quarter, which analysts see as reflecting demand ahead of GTA VI, down from 4 million a year earlier.

“We’ve modeled PlayStation profits materially ahead of the Street in the next couple of quarters, on account of the GTA VI launch,” Bernstein analyst David Dai said.

Bernstein forecasts operating profit of ￥825 billion (US$5.17 billion) at Sony’s gaming unit in the year ending March, compared with the company’s forecast of ￥800 billion.

Sony trades at about 18 times 12-month forward earnings, a discount to Nintendo’s 23 times, suggesting investors are paying a lower premium for Sony’s expected profits.

The release is bolstering Sony’s games slate after it delayed the launch of God of War Laufey by three months to May next year.

Sony is grappling with procurement challenges as the cost of memory chips has risen sharply due to the AI boom.

“I don’t get the sense that Sony has much desire to aggressively sell hardware ... the benefits Sony gets from royalties will be enormous,” Toyo Securities’ Yasuda said.

data.title: US visa holders are fed up and leaving tech jobs
data.description:
Yash Sharma decided last month that he has had enough of the US. The 36-year-old Google software engineer from India says halfway through US President Donald Trump’s second term, the constant rule changes around visas for highly skilled immigrants, the unknowns they create and the slim odds of him becoming a citizen have all become too much.

Sharma, who has had an H-1B visa for six years, says it has become hard to focus at work. And while he loves his life in San Francisco and working at the epicenter of tech and artificial intelligence (AI), he feels like he has run out of options to gain permanent residency and build a life here.

The US feels like a “golden prison,” Sharma said. He plans to move to the UK next month, even though he does not have a job there, because he was offered a visa with a clear path to staying in the country for the long term.

This month’s midterm elections delivered a rebuke of Trump’s immigration crackdown, helping Democrats win control of US Congress and prompting the president to acknowledge that his administration might have been “too tough” in deporting people who had jobs.

However, less acknowledged has been the administration’s reshaping of visa rules that for years have channeled graduates and highly skilled employees into the workforce. The newly empowered opposition would not have an easy time reversing Trump’s rule changes, which have effectively dismantled an immigration system that helped make the US a destination for the world’s best engineers and researchers.

Some of the biggest US companies are giving up on the idea anything would change soon. Payments company Flywire Corp is weighing whether to put more hiring and development work overseas, while Microsoft Corp, Adobe Inc and a handful of IT outsourcing firms have been barred from a key green-card sponsorship program as federal officials probe their practices.

The Trump administration says workers and employers have abused the immigration system for years, moving it away from its origins as a way to get highly specialized talent into the country on a temporary basis into a sprawling behemoth that has resulted in lower pay for Americans.

Trump’s appointment this month of Stephen Miller as chief of staff gives the longtime advocate of reducing all forms of immigration greater authority, while investigations into employers’ green-card sponsorships, announced last month by Vice President J.D. Vance, have added to the pressure.

“It’s a quiet dismantling of employment-based immigration,” Vialto Law immigration attorney and partner Angelo Paparelli said.

There is a growing sense that the friction and unpredictability are the new normal for the US immigration system. That is changing assumptions about the future of the US economy and forcing businesses to plan for a world in which they might not be able to bring top talent to work in their US headquarters.

Sharma says he has felt discouraged about the chances he would ever be able to convert his temporary visa into permanent residency given a huge backlog for Indian nationals. He has not left the country in a year and a half, concerned he might not be able to get back in. That has meant missing out on family visits, work conferences and trips with friends.

He sought another path to permanent residency and more stability by applying for an “extraordinary ability” visa, given to people with standout talent in their field, but was rejected after months of waiting.

The uncertainly led Sharma to consider a life outside the US. He applied for a Global Talent visa from the UK and was approved, allowing him to move to the UK without a job and begin looking for work. He says the US election results have not dissuaded him from the plan.

“I’ve seen various administrations, and to me it’s clear that there will be no actual change to the law,” he said. And even if things returned to how they were before, the difficulty of getting permanent residency would still weigh on him. “That normal still sucks,” he said.

Trump’s broad immigration crackdown started almost immediately after he took office. After campaigning on a pledge to end illegal immigration, the dragnet expanded to include narrowing paths for legal immigration, adding new regulations and steep fees.

By September last year, the popular H-1B visa program for high-skilled foreign workers became a focus, first with a presidential proclamation requiring a US$100,000 payment for certain prospective job candidates outside the US. In August, despite a court order blocking that original payment, the administration moved to impose a separate US$103,000 fee for new H-1B visa applications.

Many of Trump’s policy changes are facing legal challenges, but the chaos and confusion are difficult for companies and workers to navigate.

“It creates this profound instability for the entire immigration ecosystem,” American Immigration Lawyers Association supervisory policy and practice counsel Kate Angustia said. “We are creating a brain drain.”

data.title: Asian American women face fallout of Nvidia affair scandal
data.description:
The revelation earlier this month that billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) had extramarital affairs sent shock waves through the tech world, particularly with Asian Americans who revered him as a once-in-a-generation talent.

However, what has hit hard for Asian American women is the discourse around the allegation that Alice Huang (黃樂), a Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, was possibly a spy.

Almost immediately, videos and memes reviving tired tropes fetishizing Asian women hit social media.

“So few Asian women in general make it to the news for positive things. This is just going to continue to perpetuate negative stereotypes or biases for Asian women,” said Misa Chien, founder of a network for Asian American women leaders called The Authentic Asian. Whether or not the allegation is true, “just the news will definitely influence people’s opinions of women who have broken the ceiling or are trying to.”

Asian American women working in tech, civil rights advocacy and academia have felt a sense of dread that this ordeal would diminish how their peers are viewed and treated in their workplaces. It is a reminder that no accomplishments would completely dispel centuries-old stereotypes.

Jensen Huang has since resigned. However, the US Department of Justice has not found sufficient evidence that Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was a spy.

Among the social media posts being spread was a collage of photos showing CEOs with Asian female partners. Author May-lee Chai, who has written about the treatment of Asian women throughout history, called it “disgusting.”

Depicting them like trophy wives “implicates these spouses like they’re somehow similar to this suspected spy,” said Chai, who is also a creative writing professor at San Francisco State University.

The speed at which people glommed onto the Asian female spy narrative was shocking to April Moh, chief marketing officer for a financial technology company and board member of Stand with Asian Americans, a legal civil rights organization specializing in combating workplace anti-Asian discrimination. The chatter has also led to women sharing stories of uncomfortable interactions.

“I have women in technology who tell me that they get really weird looks and they get questioned about laptop security by their colleagues when they’re visiting China,” Moh said. “I have another person telling me that she has been jokingly asked, ‘So, are you a spy?’ by people who think that’s a joke now. It’s not funny to her or me.”

Many clients of Stand with Asian Americans are Asian women who have proved their competence, yet are still accused of being fraudulent or deceitful, the organization’s president and general counsel Rachel Lee said.

“It is deeply disturbing to see this not just unique to the Nvidia Jensen Huang case, but as a part of a long-standing dangerous narrative that Asians are perpetual foreigners, untrustworthy, disloyal,” Lee said.

On top of their integrity being questioned, Asian workers also deal with misconceptions that they cannot lead. The annual Social Tracking of Asian Americans in the US Index from The Asian American Foundation found at least half of US adults characterized Asian Americans in the workplace as “respectful” or “reliable.” Only 1 in 10 viewed them as “assertive.”

“The No. 1 theme in onboarding interviews all last week were ‘I’m mistaken for the secretary, I don’t look like the typical face of leadership,’” said Chien, talking about new members of her Asian leaders network.

Years before Chinese laborers were fully banned from entering the US under the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act, the federal government targeted immigrant Asian women. In 1875, the US Congress passed the Page Act to control immigration from “any Oriental country.” It included a specific prohibition of women coming for prostitution.

“Chinese women were deemed — and East Asian women in general — as being untrustworthy,” Chai said. “It was presumed that they would be coming for illicit means as prostitutes to the United States and that would cause harm to white men.”

By the early 20th century, the Asian woman as a seductress, spy or “dragon lady” started becoming an archetype on Hollywood screens, she added.

Suspicion toward Chinese people in the US has dramatically heightened geopolitical tensions. More than two dozen states in the last few years have proposed or enacted “alien land laws” to prevent Chinese nationals from buying property. The number of international students enrolling in US universities has fallen. And the first administration under US President Donald Trump created a plan known as the “China Initiative” to crack down on espionage by profiling Chinese professors.

Critics say that initiative contributed to the 2024 suicide of Jane Ying Wu. A neuroscientist at Northwestern University who had lived in the US for 40 years, the 60-year-old came under federal investigation in 2019. She was never charged with anything.

“This type of pernicious stereotype can actually destroy lives,” Chai said. “It’s not in any way an accurate portrait of an entire race and ethnicity.”

Jokes rooted in stereotypes under the guise of being complimentary also do not help Asian female workers, Lee added.

“Whether it’s a compliment or not, a trope is a trope,” she said. “I don’t care if it comes out of the mouth of the US president.”

data.title: Export orders increase to record high
data.description:
BEATING 2025: An official said whole-year orders could top US$1.1tn after they passed expectations due to orders received by chip designers and distributors

Export orders last month surged 78.3 percent year-on-year to a record US$123.82 billion, driven by demand for artificial intelligence (AI), high-performance computing and cloud service applications, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.

Export orders in the first 10 months of the year jumped 58.6 percent year-on-year to US$943.02 billion, hitting a record for the period and exceeding last year’s full-year total, ministry data showed.

The order momentum could continue this month and next month, Department of Statistics Director-General Huang Wei-jie (黃偉傑) told a news conference in Taipei, adding that orders this month are predicted to rise 57.6 to 62.7 percent to between US$115 billion and US$118.7 billion.

This year as a whole, export orders could top US$1.1 trillion, supported by information and communications technology, and electronic products, although reaching US$1.2 trillion would be a challenge, Huang said.

Last month’s export orders exceeded the ministry’s expectation of annual growth of up to 67 percent, thanks to large orders received by chip designers and distributors, while smartphone orders declined more slowly than expected, Huang said.

Last month, orders for information and communication technology products rose 107.2 percent annually to US$46.77 billion, driven by expansion in the AI, data centers and cloud service industries, as well as increased demand for consumer electronics, he said.

Demand was particularly strong for AI servers powered by new-generation graphics processing units and application-specific integrated circuits, he said.

“Based on the information currently available, data centers already under construction are unlikely to be halted. AI development could face some short-term volatility, but the long-term trend remains positive,” Huang said.

Orders for electronic products soared 89.8 percent year-on-year to US$53.91 billion, driven by demand for IC design, distribution and manufacturing services, as well as memory products amid booming high-performance computing applications, he said.

Orders for optical equipment fell 1.8 percent year-on-year to US$1.7 billion on weak demand for large flat-panel displays, he added.

Order momentum at traditional industries last month improved, with machinery orders rising 36.3 percent year-on-year to US$2.44 billion, driven by global semiconductor capacity expansion and demand for automation equipment, he said.

Base metal orders increased 22 percent to US$2.34 billion, supported by AI supply-chain demand for copper foil and copper-clad laminates, he said.

Orders for chemical products rose 19.5 percent year-on-year to US$1.73 billion, driven by AI supply-chain demand, while orders for plastic and rubber products increased 10.8 percent to US$1.54 billion, he added.

data.title: House describes Nvidia sales approved to China
data.description:
CHIP TRADE: Lawmakers said that more than 30% of the AI chips sent to China going to ‘military companies’ was astonishing and raised national security issues

The administration of US President Donald Trump approved shipments of nearly 900,000 advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December last year through May, the US House of Representatives Foreign Affairs Committee said on Thursday.

The approvals for 879,000 chip shipments by the US Department of Commerce included 75,000 for Alibaba (阿里巴巴), 150,000 for Tencent (騰訊), 43,000 for Baidu (百度) and 4,000 for BYD (比亞迪), all of which are on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies, the committee said.

The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the Trump administration faces heightened scrutiny following news about former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s (黃仁勳) affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has fueled renewed calls in Washington for a tougher stance on China.

Companies had sought permission to ship more than 3.4 million chips to China during the period, the documents showed.

It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X.

News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialing up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.

“The fact that over 30 percent of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the [US] Department of War [Defense] has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle.

Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict conditions and limited volumes.”

“Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China,” it said.

AMD said it “complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations, and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations.”

Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, BYD, the commerce department and the Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Former US president Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China’s military and erode the US lead in AI.

Trump in December last year gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.

Despite the approvals, questions swirled as to whether the AI chips were actually reaching Chinese shores.

In May, Reuters reported that the US had cleared about 10 companies to buy the H200, but that no deliveries had taken place.

In testimony before the committee in July, commerce department official Jeffrey Kessler said that shipments had begun, but there had been “very few.”

Several major Chinese Internet companies had each obtained about 10,000 H200 chips, Reuters has since reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

“This is the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act,” US Representative Brian Mast, chairman of the committee, said upon releasing the data, referring to 2018 legislation that expanded the commerce department’s authority to restrict the export of sensitive technologies for national security reasons.

data.title: Suit alleges Alibaba defrauded shareholders
data.description:
Alibaba (阿里巴巴) was sued on Thursday in New York by shareholders who accused the Chinese e-commerce giant of defrauding them by concealing its ties to the suspected Chinese spy whose relationship with former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) contributed to his resignation last week.

According to a proposed class action filed in Manhattan federal court, Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its annual reports in 2024, last year and this year the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business.

Shareholders cited Alibaba’s relationship with Megaspeed, a Singaporean company suspected of helping Beijing gain access to advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence (AI) chips, and whose executive Alice Huang (黃樂) had a relationship with Jensen Huang, who is not related to her.

The shareholders said that Alibaba shares fell 14 percent over four days last week because of media reports on Alibaba’s ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, including that Alibaba had become Megaspeed’s “dominant” customer.

They attributed part of the decline to a Reuters article published on Thursday last week that said Nvidia’s spy scandal could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on Chinese AI companies’ remote use of advanced processors.

Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu (吳泳銘) is also a defendant.

Nvidia itself faces several shareholder lawsuits over the spy scandal, including allegations of lax oversight by its directors.

Wu on Thursday said that Alibaba remained on track for US$100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20 percent EBITDA margin by 2030, despite US curbs on access to computing power that could affect the company’s products and services next year.

The restrictions were imposed after Jensen Huang resigned.

In June, Alibaba sued the US government over being added to a blacklist of “Chinese military companies” that the US Department of Defense published.

Last month, a federal judge in California granted Alibaba an injunction barring the US government from denying Pentagon contracts to companies whose lobbyists also work with designated Chinese military companies.

Alibaba said that restriction caused its lobbyists to retreat because they feared losing other customers and violated its right to speak to and petition the government as stipulated in the First Amendment of the US constitution.

Thursday’s lawsuit by Alibaba shareholder Withida Bihan seeks unspecified damages for holders of Alibaba’s American depositary shares between May 23, 2024, and Wednesday last week.

data.title: Probe opened over Nvidia influence on US government
data.description:
US representatives have opened a probe into what influence Nvidia was able to wield over a US Department of Commerce investigation of cloud company Megaspeed for possible illegal diversion of chips to China, according to a letter reviewed by Reuters.

In letter dated Thursday to US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, the lawmakers said they wanted to know “whether the department allowed a major American corporation that is financially and personally linked to the [US President Donald] Trump administration to interfere with enforcement activity.”

Singapore-based Megaspeed has attracted public attention since news broke that former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang (黃樂), whom US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday.

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy.

Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that operates data centers, has been under US investigation for two years, the department and the US Department of Justice said this week.

They said that commerce department investigators requested records from Nvidia in May last year about sales to the company and, with Singaporean authorities, conducted an on-site inspection in June last year at Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang.

In August last year, Nvidia contacted commerce department employees directly and requested a meeting with one of them, a commerce department official told reporters, referring to the investigators.

Nvidia told them that US Undersecretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler said the company could communicate with the employees.

“The American public and Congress deserve a full accounting of what happened,” US representatives Gregory Meeks, ranking member of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and Sydney Kamlager-Dove wrote in the letter, which requested that answers and documents be provided by Dec. 1.

A spokesperson for the commerce department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement that the bureau “conducts all enforcement strictly by the book.”

“BIS enforces aggressively across the board, including with respect to chip smuggling,” it said.

Megaspeed said it complies with all applicable laws, including US export control requirements.

An Nvidia spokesperson said that as an American company, it consults with officials at the commerce department to answer questions, provide information, and request their guidance and instructions.

“We look forward to engaging with Congress on this matter,” the company said.

data.title: SpaceX wraps up AI chip debt worth US$32 billion
data.description:
SpaceX’s US$32 billion debt deal to fund its access to artificial intelligence (AI) chips might serve as a blueprint for similar transactions as the next wave of financing tied to the AI boom gets under way.

It is likely going to be costly for the companies borrowing.

The bulk of the complex offering was sold at relatively high yields of more than 8 percent — levels that are not typically associated with investment-grade debt and reflect general concern that AI spending will not pay off.

The deal, designed to keep the borrowing off SpaceX’s balance sheet, is part of a more than US$40 billion financing that also includes bank loans.

The cash is to be used to fund the acquisition of Nvidia Corp chips by a special-purpose vehicle known as the Saturn Funding Trust and managed by an Apollo Global Management Inc entity.

Elon Musk’s rocket, satellite and AI company is to lease the equipment for about five years.

Chip-backed debt is on track to become a trillion-dollar market, eclipsing the massive borrowings used to build the data centers housing the semiconductors.

The companies at the forefront of the AI infrastructure buildout have raised hundreds of billions of dollars in the US investment-grade bond market this year. While the borrowing spree is set to continue into next year, a growing share of that financing is likely to shift toward shorter-term chip and data center debt as the market’s capacity to absorb unsecured borrowing from hyperscalers comes under strain, according to Barclays PLC.

“The unsecured market is near the limit of what it can absorb each year,” Barclays analysts including Dominique Toublan said in a recent note.

The SpaceX debt was sold on Thursday in three parts, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Apollo ran the transaction, the people said, asking not to be identified as they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Representatives for the firms and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment.

The financing included about US$25.2 billion of so-called Class A3 notes that priced at a yield of 8.259 percent, a level far higher than the average US high-grade bond yield of 5.95 percent, Bloomberg index data showed.

data.title: HSBC Taiwan hosts inaugural Trust Finance and Treating Customers Fairly Forum
data.description:
HSBC and Deloitte yesterday co-hosted the Trust Finance and Treating Customers Fairly (TCF) Forum in Taiwan. The event brought together representatives from the government, industry and academia to discuss evolving TCF practices, strengthen awareness of financial fraud, and explore ways to build a safer and more resilient financial ecosystem.

The forum focused on three key areas: ethical business conduct, conduct risk management and financial fraud prevention. Speakers examined these issues from the perspectives of policy, law enforcement, financial institutions and technological innovation. Clients and frontline financial professionals also contributed to the discussions, highlighting the importance of practical, customer-focused approaches.

Strengthening trust through collaboration

HSBC Bank (Taiwan) Ltd Chairman David Grimme and CEO Adam Chen (陳志堅) both attended the forum in person, demonstrating HSBC Taiwan’s strong commitment to treating customers fairly.

The event also welcomed Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) Vice Chairperson, Dr. Chen Yen-liang, Chen (陳彥良), the Anti-Money Laundering Office Executive Secretary and Head Prosecutor Lo Wei-Yuan (羅韋淵), the Central Counter Fraud Coordination Center Executive Secretary Wang Tsung-sheng (王琮聖), Taiwan Association of Law and Accounting President Dr. Lee Kuen-chang, and Deloitte Taiwan Consulting Businesses Senior Partner Chris Chen (陳鴻棋), who shared their insights.

Their participation reflected a shared commitment among government, industry and academia to strengthening trust and cooperation across the financial sector.

David Grimme, Chairman of HSBC Bank Taiwan, said: “Trust is the foundation of financial services. For more than 160 years, HSBC has been guided by a strong risk culture and a commitment to integrity across the organisation. These principles support our ambition to be the world’s most trusted bank.”

“Treating customers fairly is not simply a regulatory obligation. It is essential to strengthening the resilience of financial institutions and meeting our broader social responsibilities,” said Adam Chen, CEO of HSBC Taiwan. “Trust in financial services begins with putting customers first. Treating customers fairly has long been central to HSBC’s approach.

In 2026, HSBC Taiwan was ranked among the top 25% of financial institutions in the FSC’s Treating Customers Fairly assessment and received the Most Improved Award — the only bank to receive both distinctions this year.

“These recognitions reflect our commitment to integrity and our customer-centric value,” Chen added.

Speaking at the forum, Financial Supervisory Commission Vice Chairperson Yen-Liang Chen said: “Capital strength determines the scale of operations, professional expertise influences the quality of services, and public trust determines how far the financial industry can go.”

“As digitalization, product diversification and emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence continue to reshape financial services, the industry faces an increasingly complex operating environment and risk landscape, he said, adding that “balancing innovation and growth with financial stability, consumer protection and societal expectations is a shared responsibility of the financial industry and regulators.”

Tackling financial crime and trust challenges

The forum featured two keynote speeches. The Anti-Money Laundering Office Executive Secretary and Head Prosecutor Lo Wei-yuan shared insights into combating financial crime. Deloitte Taiwan Consulting Businesses Senior Partner Chris Chen further spoke about challenges to trust in the financial industry.

The forum concluded with a panel discussion involving representatives from the government, industry and academia. The session focused on three themes: trust finance, internal corporate governance and treating customers fairly.

Participants explored how information sharing between institutions and risk-based management can strengthen fraud prevention while preserving a positive customer experience. They also emphasised the role of boards and senior management in leading by example, embedding fair customer treatment into business decisions, and encouraging stronger collaboration across sectors. They noted that these combined efforts could help create a financial environment that is safer, fairer and more trusted by customers and the wider community.
